primary_topics: Chapter 22 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's annual survey of important developments on the death penalty, continuing a discussion he had included in each of his four previous books.

The record of his seventh year: no new executions, only seven convicts ever lethally injected under RA 7659, the executive's evident reluctance to implement the law, President Estrada's moratorium continued by President Arroyo through 90-day reprieves, and Congress again debating repeal through Senate Bill 2060.

The statistics from the SC Judicial Records Office -- 483 death cases reviewed, 143 affirmed, 46 acquittals and 294 modified, reduced or remanded -- and his explanation that the Court affirms only about a third of death penalties because trial courts and prosecutors overlook eight recurring legal conditions.

Nine new jurisprudential pronouncements of the year: age and relationship cannot be stipulated, the Pruna guidelines on proving a victim's age, the requirement of proper identification, sufficiency of the information, the town mayor as a non-independent counsel, the inadmissibility of oral extra-judicial confessions, the reliability of DNA testing, separate voting on guilt and penalty, and the end of illegal firearm possession as a separate offense.
sub_topics: He opens by noting that in four previous books he always included a discussion of death penalty developments, and that this volume is no exception.

Under RA 7659, Leo Echegaray was the first lethally injected on February 5, 1999, followed by Eduardo Agbayani, Dante Piandiong, Jesus Morallos, Archie Bulan, Pablito Andan and Alex Bartolome -- seven in all.

In People v. Echegaray the Court upheld the law's constitutionality by a per curiam Resolution passed 12-3, and has continued reviewing death cases, affirming 143 death impositions as of August 8, 2002.
Only those seven have actually been killed: 'It seems the executive branch of government has shown some reluctance in fully implementing the Death Penalty Law.'

President Estrada's December 11, 2000 moratorium was continued by President Arroyo, whose Memorandum of August 27, 2002 postponed the scheduled executions of Rolando Pagdayawon, Eddie Sernadilla and Filomeno Serrano by 90 days each.
Congress was again seriously discussing repeal: over 130 House members and fifteen named senators backed Senate Bill 2060 substituting thirty years' imprisonment for death.

Pagdayawon v. Secretary of Justice held that the pendency of a repeal bill does not warrant a TRO staying a final death sentence -- the remedy lies with the Office of the President -- and the Court declined to re-examine constitutionality, since the issue 'cannot be made to depend on the individual opinions of the members who compose the Court.'

He repeats that the international trend is unmistakably towards abolition, citing Article 1 of the Optional Protocol to the ICCPR, adopted by the UN on December 15, 1989 but never signed, ratified or acceded to by the Philippines.

The PAO press conference of Persida Rueda-Acosta reporting 107 convicts 'spared' created a stir on the mistaken notion that the Court had 'commuted' penalties; the Philippine Star editorial read the numbers as evidence of sloppy work by lower courts and law enforcers and as making an overhaul of criminal justice urgent.

He adds what the editorial did not: if trial courts can be wrong more often than right in imposing capital sentences, then 'there is always a probability of an erroneous death being inflicted,' so the wisdom and necessity of the penalty need review.

The eight conditions under which death cannot be imposed -- unalleged qualifying or aggravating circumstances; unproved age and relationship in incestuous rape; crimes committed before the law's effectivity on December 31, 1993; unproved age in statutory rape; drug cases without an aggravating circumstance; proof only of a lesser included crime; youthful offenders who have behaved properly; and minority as a privileged mitigating circumstance.

Pronouncement 1: People v. Agravante and People v. Sajolga hold that the complainant's age and the parties' relationship cannot be the subject of stipulation, since 'an accused cannot be condemned to suffer the extreme penalty of death on the basis of stipulations or his own admissions.'

Pronouncement 2: People v. Pruna, penned by Chief Justice Davide, canvasses eleven cases where age was not proved and eight where it was, then sets six guidelines headed by the rule that the best evidence of age is a certificate of live birth.

Pronouncement 3: People v. Escordial acquitted the accused because a police show-up was 'pointedly suggestive,' the witness had not seen her assailant's face, and her description did not match his appearance -- with a passage on the social psychology of lineup suggestibility.

Pronouncement 4: People v. Quezada upheld a conviction where the victim's unconsciousness was the direct consequence of the force alleged, since that consequence need not itself be alleged in the information.

Pronouncement 5: People v. Velarde acquitted the accused because the town mayor who served as his counsel exercised 'operational supervision and control' over the local police and so could not be the independent counsel the Constitution requires.
Pronouncement 6: People v. Felixminia held an unwritten admission to a police officer inadmissible, though the conviction stood on circumstantial evidence.

Pronouncement 7: People v. Vallejo upheld DNA evidence -- each person's DNA profile being distinct and unique -- listed the three possible results of testing, set five factors for assessing probative value, and rejected the claim that Philippine DNA testing was 'junk science,' noting the two laboratories at UP's NSRI and the NBI.

Pronouncement 8: People v. Roque explained that under Section 22 of RA 7659 the Court votes separately on guilt and on penalty, and surveyed cases where circumstances justified reducing death to reclusion perpetua.

Pronouncement 9: People v. Ladjaalam and People v. Bernal confirm that under RA 8294 illegal possession of a firearm used in another crime is no longer a separate offense, and that the amendment applies retroactively because it favors the accused.

stances.claim: The executive branch has shown reluctance to implement the Death Penalty Law fully, since only seven convicts have ever been lethally injected while the moratorium begun under President Estrada has been continued through President Arroyo's 90-day reprieves.
stances.rhetorical_move: inference drawn from an enumerated record of executions, moratoria and dated reprieves

stances.claim: The international trend is unmistakably towards the abolition of legalized killing, as Article 1 of the Optional Protocol to the ICCPR shows, even though the Philippines has not signed, ratified or acceded to it.
stances.rhetorical_move: appeal to an international movement, noted with precision about the country's non-participation

stances.claim: Because the Supreme Court affirms only about a third of the death penalties imposed below, and trial courts can be wrong more often than right, there is always a probability of an erroneous death being inflicted, so the wisdom and necessity of the penalty need review.
stances.rhetorical_move: statistics-to-doubt argument, adding to a newspaper editorial the conclusion it stopped short of drawing

stances.claim: Death may never rest on stipulations or admissions: the victim's age and her relationship to the offender must be alleged in the information and proven beyond reasonable doubt, because the strictness of the rule is warranted by the seriousness of the penalty.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal restatement supported by paired cases and the elements-of-the-offense rationale

stances.claim: DNA testing in the Philippines is scientific and credible rather than 'junk science,' though courts must weigh how samples were collected and handled, the possibility of contamination, adherence to proper procedure, and the analyst's qualifications.
stances.rhetorical_move: reliability defense paired with a checklist of safeguards, citing local laboratories and expert papers

stances.claim: The pendency of a repeal bill in Congress does not warrant a restraining order against a final death sentence; the remedy lies with the Office of the President, and constitutionality cannot be made to depend on the individual opinions of the Court's changing membership.
stances.rhetorical_move: separation-of-remedies reporting of the Court's holding in Pagdayawon

notable_anecdotes: He dates the writing of the book precisely -- 'as of the writing of this book on October 10, 2002' -- while reporting that no executions had by then been carried out under President Arroyo.

He recounts the public uproar after the PAO's August 7, 2002 press conference, when media reported 107 convicts 'spared' and listeners wrongly believed the Supreme Court had 'commuted' their penalties.

He quotes the Philippine Star's editorial blaming sloppy work by lower-court judges and law enforcers, then adds the conclusion the paper omitted: that the wisdom and necessity of the death penalty itself needed review.

He cites the scientific papers presented at the Third Convention and Seminar of the Philippine Judges Association on June 11, 1999, and Dr. Saturnina Halos's paper proposing that the justice system accept DNA tests as a reliable investigative tool.

He notes that People v. Escordial turned partly on the social psychology of identification -- witnesses who 'probably will feel foolish if they cannot identify anyone' and therefore choose someone despite residual uncertainty.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' continues the running survey of death penalty developments that Panganiban had included in each of his four previous books. He records that under RA 7659 only seven convicts have ever been lethally injected -- Leo Echegaray first, on February 5, 1999 -- and that although People v. Echegaray upheld the law 12-3 and the Court had affirmed 143 death impositions as of August 8, 2002, 'the executive branch of government has shown some reluctance in fully implementing' it: President Estrada's December 2000 moratorium was continued by President Arroyo, whose August 27, 2002 memorandum granted 90-day reprieves. Congress was again debating repeal through Senate Bill 2060, while Pagdayawon v. Secretary of Justice held that a pending bill cannot justify staying a final sentence and declined to revisit constitutionality. He restates that 'the international trend is unmistakably towards the abolition of legalized killing,' citing the Optional Protocol to the ICCPR. Against a PAO report that 107 convicts had been 'spared,' he supplies the fuller figures from the Judicial Records Office -- 483 cases reviewed, 143 affirmed, 46 acquitted, 294 modified or remanded -- so that only about a third of capital sentences survive, and argues that if trial courts can be wrong more often than right 'there is always a probability of an erroneous death being inflicted.' He then lists eight conditions barring a death sentence and nine new pronouncements of his seventh year: age and relationship cannot be stipulated; People v. Pruna's six guidelines on proving age; the suggestive show-up in People v. Escordial; sufficiency of the information in Quezada; the town mayor as a disqualified counsel in Velarde; the inadmissibility of unwritten confessions in Felixminia; the reliability of DNA testing in Vallejo; separate voting on guilt and penalty in Roque; and the retroactive effect of RA 8294 on illegal firearm possession.
